text:
Recent work supports history interventions for diagnosing sequential recommenders. [CoDeR (AAAI 2025)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/33379) models demand shifts obscured by noise and bias through demand extraction and counterfactual adjustment. [Scarcelli et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) search for minimal history edits that change recommendations using genetic algorithms. These approaches motivate perturbation diagnostics, but ranking sensitivity alone does not establish real user intent or causal preference change.

Strong controls matter: [Spotify Research (2026)](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) reports pairwise transition models outperforming SASRec/eSASRec reproductions on four of five benchmarks, showing that recency and item transitions can explain strong performance without joint sequence modeling. [Beyond Top-1 (RecSys 2025; IJCAI 2026 extended abstract)](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2026/926) finds ranking-aware top-k explanation evaluation more consistent than top-1 flips. Suggested diagnostic design: use training-history prefixes with subsequent training interactions as targets; compare retaining recent suffixes, deleting recent events, shuffling order while fixing the last item, and deleting repeated themes derived only from titles/descriptions. Pair targeted deletions with equal-count random removals matched on position and popularity; include popularity, last-item transition, and recency-weighted pairwise baselines. Measure paired changes in target rank, HR@10, and top-10 overlap, with user-bootstrap confidence intervals separately for all four datasets. Keep candidate sets fixed across interventions and distinguish sensitivity from improved next-item prediction. This protocol is a synthesis of the literature, not a reported experimental result.
